tools.name: Chat API Payload Builder
tools.description: Turn a system prompt and a conversation into a ready-to-send request body.
tools.lede: Write the conversation in plain text; get correct JSON for the OpenAI or Anthropic API, plus a curl command.
tools.inputLabel: Conversation — prefix lines with system:, user: or assistant:
tools.sample:
system: You are a concise assistant. Answer in British English.
user: What is the difference between a queue and a topic?
assistant: A queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer.
user: And a topic?

tools.name: JSONL Toolkit
tools.description: Validate, convert and inspect JSON Lines — the format fine-tuning and log pipelines use.
tools.lede: JSONL is one JSON document per line. This validates every line individually and tells you exactly which one is broken.

tools.name: LLM Cost Calculator
tools.description: Estimate what a prompt, a batch or a month of traffic will cost.
tools.lede: Paste your prompt to count its tokens, set the rates, and see the cost per call and at volume.
tools.inputLabel: Prompt (optional — or type a token count in the options)
tools.sample: Summarise the attached support ticket and classify it as bug, question or feature request.

options.label: Rate preset
options.hint: Indicative list prices — always confirm against the provider.

tools.name: LLM Token Counter
tools.description: Count tokens exactly with the real BPE tokenizer, and see how the text splits.
tools.lede: Real BPE tokenisation running in your browser — not a characters-divided-by-four guess. Nothing is sent anywhere.
tools.footnote: Exact for OpenAI models using these encodings. Anthropic, Google and Meta use different tokenizers and do not publish a browser-usable one — for those, treat this as a close estimate (usually within about 10%). Chat APIs also add a few tokens per message for role framing, which this does not count.
tools.sample: You are a helpful assistant. Summarise the following in three bullet points, using British English spelling and keeping each bullet under twenty words.

tools.name: Prompt Template Renderer
tools.description: Fill {{variables}} in a prompt template and see the token cost of the result.
tools.lede: Keeps prompt templates and their test values in one place, and tells you which placeholders you forgot.

options.label: Fail if a placeholder has no value

tools.name: .env Converter
tools.description: Convert between .env, JSON, YAML, docker-compose and shell exports.
tools.lede: The conversion you do by hand every time you move config between a .env file, a compose file and a Kubernetes manifest.
tools.footnote: A ConfigMap is not a secret — its values are stored unencrypted and are visible to anyone who can read the namespace. Put credentials in a Secret (or an external secret store) instead.
tools.sample:
# application
NODE_ENV=production
PORT=8080
LOG_LEVEL=debug

# database
DATABASE_URL="postgres://user:pass@db:5432/app"
DB_POOL_SIZE=10
FEATURE_FLAGS=a,b,c

tools.name: CIDR / Subnet Calculator
tools.description: Work out network, broadcast, host range and size from a CIDR block.
tools.lede: Also tells you whether an address falls inside the block — the question you actually have when debugging a security group.

tools.name: cURL Converter
tools.description: Turn a curl command into fetch, Python, Go, PowerShell or HTTPie.
tools.lede: Paste what you copied from the browser network tab ("Copy as cURL") and get working code in another language.

tools.name: Duration Converter
tools.description: Convert between 1h30m, 5400s, ISO 8601 durations and milliseconds.
tools.lede: Accepts Go-style (1h30m), plain seconds, ISO 8601 (PT1H30M) and colon notation (01:30:00).

tools.name: HTTP Reference
tools.description: Searchable status codes and MIME types, with what they actually mean.
tools.lede: Type a code, a word or a file extension.

tools.name: ID Decoder
tools.description: Pull the timestamp out of a UUID, ULID, ObjectId or Snowflake ID.
tools.lede: Most identifiers you meet in a database or a log carry a creation time. Paste one and this works out which format it is and when it was made.

tools.name: JWT Signer
tools.description: Build and sign a JSON Web Token with HS256, HS384 or HS512.
tools.lede: For creating test tokens against a service you control. Pairs with the JWT Decoder.
tools.footnote: HS256 secrets should be at least 256 bits of real entropy — a short passphrase is brute-forceable offline from a single captured token. Tokens minted here are for testing; do not use this to issue anything a real user relies on, and never paste a production signing secret into a web page.

tools.name: Kubernetes Quantity Converter
tools.description: Translate 512Mi, 1.5Gi, 250m and friends into numbers you can reason about.
tools.lede: Mi is 1024-based, M is 1000-based, and mixing them up is how you end up with a pod that OOMs. One line per quantity.

tools.name: Line Ending & Whitespace Inspector
tools.description: Find CRLF/LF mixes, BOMs, trailing spaces and tab/space inconsistency.
tools.lede: The reason a diff shows every line as changed, or a shell script fails with a mysterious \r. Paste the file to see what is really in it.
tools.sample:
first line
second line
third line with trailing space   
	fourth line indented with a tab
    fifth line indented with spaces

tools.name: Markdown Table Formatter
tools.description: Align a Markdown table, or build one from CSV, TSV or JSON.
tools.lede: Paste a ragged Markdown table to line it up, or paste CSV/TSV/JSON to turn it into one.
tools.inputLabel: Markdown table, CSV, TSV or JSON array
tools.sample:
| Tool | Language | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Parquet viewer | JS | reads real files |
| Service Bus | Python + Node | needs the relay |
| Hashes | JS | verified against hashlib |

tools.name: Mock Data Generator
tools.description: Generate realistic test rows as JSON, CSV or SQL inserts.
tools.lede: Pick the fields you need and get however many rows, ready to paste into a seed script or a test.
tools.footnote: The names are borrowed from computing pioneers, and the addresses and phone numbers are structurally valid but fictional. Do not use generated emails to send anything.

tools.name: Semver Checker
tools.description: Compare versions and test them against ranges like ^1.2.0 or >=2 <3.
tools.lede: Answers "does this version match that range" without installing anything — including the prerelease rules people get wrong.

tools.name: Unicode Inspector
tools.description: Reveal invisible characters, smart quotes and homoglyphs hiding in text.
tools.lede: When a string comparison fails for no visible reason, the answer is usually in here — a non-breaking space, a smart quote, a zero-width joiner or a Cyrillic lookalike.
tools.sample: Hello​world — "smart quotes" and a non-breaking space, plus Cyrillic а

tools.name: .gitignore Generator
tools.description: Build a .gitignore from stacks, and check what a pattern would match.
tools.lede: Pick the stacks you use — the common editor, OS and secret patterns are always included.

options.label: Stacks (comma separated)
options.hint: node, python, dotnet, java, go, rust, php, ruby, flutter, terraform, docker

tools.name: Docker Compose Validator
tools.description: Validate a compose file and flag port clashes, missing images and risky settings.
tools.lede: Parses the YAML, then checks the things a schema will not: duplicate host ports, services depending on names that do not exist, and containers given more privilege than they need.
tools.sample:
version: "3.8"
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - api
    environment:
      - DB_PASSWORD=hunter2
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:3000"
    privileged: true
    volumes:
      - /:/host
    restart: always
  worker:
    image: myapp/worker
    depends_on:
      - queue

tools.name: Dockerfile Linter
tools.description: Catch cache-busting layer order, missing USER, latest tags and other Dockerfile mistakes.
tools.lede: The checks that actually bite: images that rebuild from scratch on every code change, containers running as root, and unpinned tags.
tools.footnote: These are heuristics over the instruction list, not a full parse — heredocs, line continuations inside strings and BuildKit-specific syntax may confuse them. For CI, run hadolint as well.
tools.sample:
FROM node:latest

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .
RUN npm install
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl

ADD https://example.com/tool.tar.gz /tmp/

ENV API_KEY=sk-supersecret

EXPOSE 3000
CMD npm start

tools.name: GitHub Actions Checker
tools.description: Lint a workflow for unpinned actions, script injection and missing permissions.
tools.lede: Includes the script-injection check — interpolating ${{ github.event... }} straight into a run block lets a pull request title execute code in your runner.

    branches: [main]

      - uses: some/action@main
      - name: Greet

      - name: Deploy
        run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          TOKEN: ghp_hardcodedtokenvalue123456

tools.description: Check manifests for missing limits, root containers, latest tags and probe gaps.

tools.footnote: This checks structure and production-readiness conventions. It does not validate against the Kubernetes OpenAPI schema — for that use kubectl apply --dry-run=server, kubeconform or kubeval.

tools.description: Reformat and normalise YAML with consistent indentation and quoting.

tools.footnote: Re-emitting normalises the document: comments are not preserved, because YAML comments are not part of the parsed data. If you need comments kept, format by hand or use a comment-preserving tool such as yq.

tools.name: Bcrypt Checker
tools.description: Verify whether a password matches a bcrypt hash.
tools.lede: Paste the hash and the candidate password to test them against each other.

tools.name: Bcrypt Generator
tools.description: Hash a password with bcrypt at a chosen cost factor.
tools.lede: Bcrypt is deliberately slow and salts automatically, which is what makes it suitable for passwords.
tools.footnote: Bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes. If you need to support longer passwords, pre-hash with SHA-256 first, or use argon2id instead. Hashes generated here are computed in your browser and never leave it — but do not paste a real production password into any web page, including this one.

options.label: Cost factor (rounds)
options.hint: Each +1 doubles the work. 10–12 is typical; 15 takes several seconds.

tools.name: Hash Generator
tools.description: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, Keccak and RIPEMD-160 digests of text or a file.
tools.lede: Every algorithm is computed at once so you can compare against whichever checksum you were given. Files are hashed locally — nothing is uploaded.
tools.footnote: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes — practical collision attacks exist for both. They are still fine for non-adversarial uses like cache keys, ETags and detecting accidental corruption. For signatures, certificates or password storage use SHA-256 or better (and for passwords specifically, bcrypt/argon2 rather than a raw hash).
tools.sample: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

tools.name: HMAC Generator
tools.description: Keyed-hash message authentication codes over any supported digest.
tools.lede: RFC 2104 HMAC. Handy for verifying webhook signatures from Stripe, GitHub, Slack and friends.
tools.footnote: When you verify a signature in production code, compare with a constant-time equality function (crypto.timingSafeEqual, hmac.compare_digest) rather than ===, so an attacker cannot learn the correct value from response timing.
tools.sample: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

tools.name: JWT Decoder
tools.description: Decode a JSON Web Token and verify its HMAC signature.
tools.lede: Splits the token, decodes the header and claims, renders the timestamps and — with a secret — checks the signature.
tools.footnote: Decoding a JWT does not authenticate it — anyone can read and rewrite the claims. Only a verified signature makes a token trustworthy, and the server must pin the expected algorithm rather than trusting the token's own alg field.

tools.name: Base32 Decoder
tools.description: Decode Base32 back into readable text.
tools.lede: Decodes Base32 to bytes, then interprets those bytes as UTF-8 text.

tools.name: Base32 Encoder
tools.description: Encode text or a file into Base32.
tools.lede: UTF-8 encodes the text, then renders the bytes as Base32. RFC 4648 Base32 uses A–Z and 2–7 only, so it survives case-insensitive systems like DNS and TOTP secrets.

tools.name: Base32 to HEX
tools.description: Convert Base32 directly into hexadecimal.
tools.lede: Decodes Base32 to raw bytes and re-renders them as hex — no text interpretation in between.

tools.name: Base58 Decoder
tools.description: Decode Base58 back into readable text.
tools.lede: Decodes Base58 to bytes, then interprets those bytes as UTF-8 text.

tools.name: Base58 Encoder
tools.description: Encode text or a file into Base58.
tools.lede: UTF-8 encodes the text, then renders the bytes as Base58. Bitcoin-style Base58 omits 0, O, I and l to avoid visual ambiguity. There is no padding.

tools.name: Base58 to HEX
tools.description: Convert Base58 directly into hexadecimal.
tools.lede: Decodes Base58 to raw bytes and re-renders them as hex — no text interpretation in between.

tools.name: Base64 Decoder
tools.description: Decode Base64 back into readable text.
tools.lede: Decodes Base64 to bytes, then interprets those bytes as UTF-8 text.

tools.name: Base64 Encoder
tools.description: Encode text or a file into Base64.
tools.lede: UTF-8 encodes the text, then renders the bytes as Base64. Base64 packs 3 bytes into 4 characters, so output is about 33% larger than the input.

tools.name: Base64 to File
tools.description: Decode a Base64 string or data URI back into a downloadable file.
tools.lede: Paste Base64 or a full data: URI. Images are previewed; anything else can be saved straight to disk.

tools.name: Base64 to HEX
tools.description: Convert Base64 directly into hexadecimal.
tools.lede: Decodes Base64 to raw bytes and re-renders them as hex — no text interpretation in between.

tools.name: File to Base64
tools.description: Encode any file as a Base64 string or a ready-to-use data URI.
tools.lede: Pick a file with the File button. Everything stays in your browser — nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: HEX to Base32
tools.description: Convert hexadecimal bytes into Base32.
tools.lede: Parses hex into raw bytes and encodes them as Base32. Separators and 0x prefixes are tolerated.

tools.name: HEX to Base58
tools.description: Convert hexadecimal bytes into Base58.
tools.lede: Parses hex into raw bytes and encodes them as Base58. Separators and 0x prefixes are tolerated.

tools.name: HEX to Base64
tools.description: Convert hexadecimal bytes into Base64.
tools.lede: Parses hex into raw bytes and encodes them as Base64. Separators and 0x prefixes are tolerated.

tools.name: Passphrase Generator
tools.description: Generate memorable multi-word passphrases with real entropy figures.
tools.lede: Diceware-style passphrases drawn from a 2,413-word list (11.24 bits per word).
tools.footnote: Capitalising words or appending a digit adds far less entropy than one extra word — if you want it stronger, add a word.

tools.name: Password Generator
tools.description: Generate strong random passwords with a live entropy read-out.
tools.lede: Generated with crypto.getRandomValues in your browser. Nothing is transmitted or stored.
tools.footnote: Entropy assumes an attacker knows your exact generator settings — the honest worst case. Crack times are for a fast hash; a password stored with bcrypt or argon2 takes far longer to attack.

tools.name: PIN Generator
tools.description: Generate random numeric PINs, optionally with no repeated digits.
tools.lede: Uniform random digits — not the pseudo-random Math.random most generators use.
tools.footnote: A numeric PIN is inherently low-entropy — a 6-digit PIN has only ~20 bits. PINs are only safe where the number of attempts is strictly rate-limited (a phone, a bank card), never as a standalone password.

tools.name: Random Data Generator
tools.description: Random integers, decimals, hex bytes, colours and picks from a list.
tools.lede: Cryptographically secure random values in whatever shape you need.

tools.name: UUID Generator
tools.description: Generate UUID v4, time-ordered v7, or v1-style identifiers in bulk.
tools.lede: v4 is fully random. v7 embeds a millisecond timestamp in the high bits, so IDs sort chronologically — much kinder to database indexes.

tools.name: Colour Converter
tools.description: Convert between HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV and CMYK with contrast checking.
tools.lede: Accepts hex, rgb(), hsl() and CSS colour names. Also reports WCAG contrast against black and white.
tools.footnote: WCAG 2.1 requires 4.5:1 for normal body text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+, or 14pt bold). AAA raises those to 7:1 and 4.5:1.

tools.name: Mermaid Generator
tools.description: Build flowcharts, sequence diagrams, ERDs and mind maps from plain lists or CSV.
tools.lede: Write the structure as indented lines, arrows or CSV — get valid Mermaid you can paste into a README.
tools.sample:
Request received -> Validate payload
Validate payload -> Enrich from cache
Validate payload -> Reject
Enrich from cache -> Publish to Service Bus
Publish to Service Bus -> Acknowledge

tools.name: Mermaid Validator
tools.description: Check a Mermaid diagram parses, and get the error line when it does not.
tools.lede: Runs the real Mermaid parser. Useful before committing a diagram to a README, where a syntax error just renders as a grey box.
tools.sample:
flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B{Valid?}
    B -->|yes| C[Process]
    B -->|no| D[Reject]
    C --> E[End
    D --> E

tools.name: Mermaid Viewer
tools.description: Write Mermaid diagrams with a live preview and export to SVG or PNG.

tools.name: QR Code Generator
tools.description: Turn text, a URL, wifi credentials or a vCard into a downloadable QR code.
tools.lede: Generated locally — the content never leaves your browser. Download as PNG or SVG.
tools.footnote: Useful content formats — wifi: WIFI:T:WPA;S:NetworkName;P:password;; · phone: tel:+441234567890 · email: mailto:me@example.com?subject=Hi · SMS: SMSTO:+44123:message

options.label: Error correction
options.hint: Higher correction survives damage but needs a denser code.

tools.name: QR Code Reader
tools.description: Extract the text from a QR code image without uploading it anywhere.
tools.lede: Choose a PNG, JPEG or WebP containing a QR code. Decoding happens locally in your browser.

tools.name: Cron Expression Parser
tools.description: Explain a cron schedule in plain English and list the next run times.
tools.lede: Five fields (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week), or six with a leading seconds field.
tools.footnote: When both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, standard cron fires if either matches — a common source of surprise. Quartz extensions (L, W, #) are not supported here.

tools.name: Timestamp Converter
tools.description: Convert between Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 and human-readable dates.
tools.lede: Paste a Unix timestamp (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds) or any date string — the unit is detected automatically. Leave it empty for "now".

tools.name: My IP Address
tools.description: Look up your public IP address and the network it belongs to.
tools.lede: Your public IP is only visible to an outside server, so this one tool has to make a network request. Nothing happens until you press the button.
tools.footnote: This is the only tool on the site that sends anything off your machine. It queries ipapi.co, which necessarily sees your IP address in order to report it back. Geolocation from an IP is approximate and often wrong by tens of kilometres — it reflects your ISP, not your device.

tools.name: My User Agent
tools.description: Inspect your browser, platform, screen and locale — all read locally.
tools.lede: Everything here is read from your own browser. No request is made to any server.

tools.name: Service Bus Consumer
tools.description: Receive and settle messages from an Azure Service Bus queue or subscription.

tools.name: Service Bus Publisher
tools.description: Publish messages to an Azure Service Bus queue or topic using a connection string.

tools.name: Architecture
tools.description: Designs or reviews system architecture - component boundaries, data flow, scaling, failure modes, trade-offs. Use for "how should we build X", "review this design", or evaluating an architectural change. For a concrete implementation plan use Plan; for building it use nikbot-dev.

tools.name: Bug Hunt
tools.description: Diagnoses a specific defect - reproduces it, isolates the cause, explains the mechanism, and proposes a minimal fix. Use for a failing test, a stack trace, a crash, or "this works here but not there". For a broad hunt across unchanged code use nikbot-review; for slowness rather than wrongness use nikbot-perf.

tools.name: Developer
tools.description: Implements a described feature, change or fix end to end - writes the code, matches existing conventions, and verifies it builds and passes tests. Use when the user wants something built rather than analysed. For diagnosing an unknown defect first use nikbot-bug; for writing tests for existing code use the nikbot-unit agents.

tools.name: Documentation
tools.description: Writes and updates documentation - READMEs, API references, architecture notes, runbooks, changelogs, code comments. Use for "document this", "update the README", or when a change needs its docs brought in line. For explaining code to yourself rather than producing a document use nikbot-explain.

tools.name: Explain
tools.description: Explains how an unfamiliar codebase, module or mechanism works, so you can work in it. Use for "how does this work", "where do I start", onboarding, or tracing a flow end to end. For a short description use nikbot-summary; for judging the design use nikbot-arch.

tools.name: Performance
tools.description: Investigates slowness or excessive resource use by measuring first - profiles, finds the real bottleneck, proposes changes with expected effect. Use for "this is slow", "why does this use so much memory", or evaluating a performance claim. For wrong results rather than slow ones use nikbot-bug.

tools.name: Pull Request Review
tools.description: Reviews a complete branch or pull request - every commit, the full diff against the base, the description, and merge risk. Use for "review this PR", "review my branch before I raise it", or when given a PR number or URL. For uncommitted work in progress use nikbot-review instead.

tools.name: Requirements Review
tools.description: Reviews requirements, specs, tickets and acceptance criteria for ambiguity, gaps, testability and contradictions - before anyone builds them. Use for "is this ticket ready", "review this spec", or "what is missing from these requirements". For designing the solution use nikbot-arch.

tools.name: Research
tools.description: Investigates an open question across the codebase and the web and returns a sourced answer with trade-offs. Use for "how should we do X", "what are the options for Y", "how does library Z handle this", or comparing approaches. For locating code in this repo use Explore; for a system design use nikbot-arch.

tools.name: Code Review
tools.description: Reviews uncommitted or staged code changes for correctness, security and maintainability. Use when the user asks to review their work, check a diff before committing, or find problems in changes they just made. For a whole branch or a GitHub PR use nikbot-pr instead; for a security-only pass use nikbot-security.

tools.name: Sanity Check
tools.description: Fast pre-commit gate - builds, runs tests, and scans the diff for obvious mistakes like secrets, debug leftovers and stray files. Use before committing or pushing when you want a quick pass/fail, not a considered review. For a real review use nikbot-review.

tools.name: Security Review
tools.description: Security audit with an attacker-first mindset - untrusted input, authn/authz, secrets, injection, dependency CVEs. Use for "is this secure", auditing a feature that handles user input or credentials, or a pre-release security pass. For general correctness review use nikbot-review.

tools.name: Summary
tools.description: Condenses something into a short, accurate summary - a file, a directory, a diff, a log, a document, or recent commits. Use for "what does this do", "summarise this", "what changed". For understanding a module well enough to work in it use nikbot-explain; for judging quality use nikbot-review.

tools.name: Test Strategy
tools.description: Analyses test coverage and designs a test strategy - what is untested, which tests are weak, what should be tested at which level. Use for "what tests do we need", "is this well tested", or planning a test suite. To actually write the tests use nikbot-unit-dotnet or nikbot-unit-python.

tools.name: Triage
tools.description: Reads logs, traces, crash dumps and monitoring output to work out what happened and what to do next. Use for "here are the logs from the failure", incident triage, or making sense of a long noisy log. To then diagnose the defect in code use nikbot-bug.

tools.name: Unit Tests (.NET)
tools.description: Writes unit tests for C#/.NET code using the project's existing framework (xUnit, NUnit or MSTest). Use for "write tests for this class" in a .NET repo. For deciding what should be tested use nikbot-test; for Python use nikbot-unit-python.

tools.name: Unit Tests (Python)
tools.description: Writes unit tests for Python code using the project's existing framework (pytest or unittest). Use for "write tests for this module" in a Python repo. For deciding what should be tested use nikbot-test; for .NET use nikbot-unit-dotnet.

tools.name: Upgrade (.NET)
tools.description: Upgrades NuGet packages and .NET target frameworks - CVE audit, breaking changes, transitive resolution, staged verification. Use for dependency or framework upgrades in a .NET repo. For other ecosystems use nikbot-upgrade or nikbot-upgrade-python.

tools.name: Upgrade (Python)
tools.description: Upgrades Python dependencies and the interpreter version - CVE audit, breaking changes, resolver conflicts, staged verification. Use for dependency or Python version upgrades in a Python repo. For other ecosystems use nikbot-upgrade or nikbot-upgrade-dotnet.

tools.name: Dependency Upgrade
tools.description: Plans and performs dependency upgrades - reads changelogs, finds breaking changes and CVEs, sequences the work, verifies after each step. Use for "update our dependencies", "are we on anything vulnerable", or upgrading a specific package. Language-specific variants exist for .NET and Python.
